title: AI-generated feedback on writing: insights into efficacy and ENL student preference
venue: International Journal of Educational Technology in Higher Education
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether generative AI can be used effectively as an automated writing evaluation tool in English as a new language (ENL) writing instruction, and whether students prefer AI-generated feedback to feedback from a human tutor. The authors focus on GPT-4/ChatGPT-generated feedback on student writing, motivated by broader concerns about how generative AI may affect instructional practice, feedback quality, and student learning in education.

The study combines two related investigations conducted over a six-week period at a small liberal arts university in the Asia-Pacific region. In Study 1, 48 ENL university students were split into an experimental group that received GPT-4 feedback and a control group that received feedback from a human tutor; writing outcomes were measured using pre/post tests and weekly writing tasks. In Study 2, a separate group of 43 ENL students received both AI and human feedback on weekly assignments and completed repeated preference surveys plus open-ended responses about the two feedback modes.

Results from Study 1 showed no significant difference in writing gains between the AI-feedback group and the human-tutor group, suggesting that GPT-4 feedback did not outperform human feedback but also did not harm learning outcomes. Results from Study 2 showed a near-even split in student preference, with some students valuing the clarity, specificity, and consistency of AI feedback, while others preferred human interaction, engagement, and the ability to ask follow-up questions. The authors conclude that AI-generated feedback may be used in ENL writing instruction without reducing learning outcomes, but they recommend a blended model that combines the strengths of both AI and human tutoring.

identified_tools.name: ChatGPT
identified_tools.description: OpenAI's GPT-based chatbot interface for interacting with large language models, capable of generating and revising natural-language text, including feedback on writing.
identified_tools.use_case: Used to generate individualized corrective feedback on ENL students' weekly writing assignments (GPT-4 via ChatGPT) and to compare AI-generated feedback with human tutor feedback over six weeks.

findings.finding_summary: In Study 1 (n=48; analyzable n=48 minus 1 posttest-only case excluded), ENL students who received GPT-4-generated feedback showed no significant difference in writing gains compared with students who received human tutor feedback. findings.measure: Pretest/posttest writing scores on an analytic rubric (content, coherence, language use, sources and evidence; max score 40)

findings.finding_summary: In Study 2 (n=43; weekly survey responses varying from 32 to 41), student preferences for GPT-4 feedback versus human tutor feedback were roughly split. The six-week average preference counts were 18 for human tutor feedback and 19.667 for AI-generated feedback, with questionnaire means slightly favoring human feedback on satisfaction, clarity, helpfulness, and overall preference but all means remaining above 4 in most weeks.
findings.measure: Weekly Likert-scale preference/satisfaction survey and open-ended responses

quality_tier_rationale: This is a quasi-experimental longitudinal study with repeated measures and a separate preference survey, but it is not a randomized controlled trial. The mixed-methods design and modest sample sizes support moderate confidence, though causal inference is limited.
impact_tier_rationale: The main efficacy finding is null: GPT-4 feedback did not outperform human tutor feedback, and the reported effect sizes are small. Student preference was mixed rather than strongly positive or negative, indicating limited demonstrated impact.
